title: Protectionist Winston Peters named New Zealand deputy PM and foreign minister
text: Veteran protectionist politician Winston Peters was named New Zealand's new deputy prime minister and foreign minister on Wednesday, saying he would push for a greater voice in international affairs, including on North Korea. Peters visited North Korea in 2005, when he was foreign minister in an earlier New Zealand government. As leader of the New Zealand First party, Peters handed government to the Labour party through a coalition deal after a closely contested election on Sept. 23 failed to produce a majority for either the governing National party or Labour. Peters and Labour Prime Minister-designate Jacinda Ardern have found common ground in "fortress New Zealand"-type policies. Both aim to curb immigration, renegotiate certain trade deals and adjust the role of the central bank. Ardern also wants to bar overseas buyers from purchasing existing homes as prices become increasingly unaffordable for local residents. A bill banning such purchases will be introduced by Christmas, Ardern told a workers' conference on Wednesday. But restrictions on trade and foreign ownership could damage New Zealand's reputation as an open economy and antagonize countries such as China. Trade between the two countries has grown to more than NZ$20 billion ($14.4 billion) a year, and Chinese President Xi Jinping has called the relationship unprecedented in its depth. While Peters had been expected to be offered the deputy role after securing the balance of power, his appointment as both deputy prime minister and foreign minister came as a surprise. Richard Shaw, a politics professor at Massey University, said Peters was a "conservative economic nationalist." "One of the things we've seen from him over the last couple of weeks is the concern with the extent that relatively unbridled free trade has on his constituents," Shaw said.

title: Trump Vows To "Renovate" The Bill of Rights
text: If anybody in this "great" land knows a thing or two about renovation, it may well be presidential hopeful Donald J. Trump. A real estate veteran of several decades, Trump has surely renovated his share of properties, buildings and even golf courses. His newest project, though, might be his most ambitious yet: the Bill of Rights itself. "Look at this thing," The Donald said as he held up a copy of the seminal American document in front of a crowd of reporters. "It's old. I mean, it's old, like really old. You hear what I'm saying? It is old." Asked what he intended to do with the document, Trump proposed a "renovation" of the foundational document "just like he would any of [his] older buildings that didn't cut the mustard anymore. I mean, Ivana wasn't cutting it anymore, so I got Marla Maples. New is better. I think we all know that, new is better. New equals better. Sometimes you have to tear something down to make something new, right? And then it's all better." Asked what exactly he meant by "tearing down the document" that forms the basis of this country's inalienable rights, Trump went on, "Hey look, I don't know when this thing was written, probably a long time ago, like in the 1920's or something, but it doesn't make any sense anymore. I have a real problem with an old, stinky document telling me how to live my life. If we're gonna make America great again, the first thing we have to do is make these document new again, and that's what I'm gonna do on the first day in office. Bingo-bango, new document for the new America."

title: Mass grave with ten bodies found in Myanmar, army newspaper says
text: Myanmar authorities have discovered 10 bodies buried in a mass grave at the edge of a village in Rakhine State, the military-run newspaper Myawady reported on Tuesday, a day after the army said it had opened an investigation at the site. Around 650,000 Rohingya Muslims have fled Rakhine state for neighboring Bangladesh in recent months following a violent crackdown there by Myanmar security forces in response to militant attacks. Rights monitors have accused troops of atrocities during the crackdown, including killings, mass rape and arson. The United States has said it amounted to "ethnic cleansing." The Myanmar military has said its own internal investigation cleared security forces of all accusations of atrocities. A team that included police, a local administrator, a judge and a doctor examined the grave site at the village of Inn Din, about 50 km (30 miles) north of the state capital Sittwe, on Tuesday and found 10 unidentified bodies, Myawady said. "This group is continuing the process of investigation to uncover the truth," the report said. Military officials could not immediately be reached for further comment. The discovery of a mass grave near a cemetery in the village was announced on Monday in a statement on the official Facebook page of the army commander-in-chief. The village lies in Maungdaw township, one of the areas hit hardest by the violence that has led the United Nations' top human rights official to allege that Myanmar's security forces may have committed genocide against the Rohingya. Myanmar's armed forces launched what they called "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine, where many members of the stateless Muslim minority lived, after Rohingya militants attacked 30 police posts and an army base on Aug. 25.

title: Neapolitan pizza making awarded world heritage status
text: The art of Neapolitan pizza making was granted world heritage status on Thursday, joining an Iranian horse-riding game and Dutch windmills on UNESCO's culture list. UNESCO added the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuoli, or pizza makers, to the world body's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. It congratulated Italy in a tweet after a meeting in Jeju, South Korea, where the decision was taken. Italy had argued that the practice of the pizzaiuoli - preparing and flipping the dough, topping it and baking it in a wood-fired oven - was part of the country's cultural and gastronomic tradition. In Rome, pizzeria owner Romano Fiore welcomed the decision. "I am honored, like all Italians and Neapolitans are...pizza has centuries of history," he said. The archetypal Neapolitan pizza has a fairly thin crust except for the rim, which puffs up when baked like a tiny bicycle tire. It is made in a wood-burning brick oven and comes in two classic versions: Marinara (tomato, garlic, oregano and oil) and, the best known, Margherita (tomato, mozzarella, oil and basil), which carries the red, white and green colors of the Italian flag. According to tradition, the Margherita pizza was created in 1889 by a local chef in honor of Queen Margherita, who was visiting Naples, south of Rome on Italy's Tyrrhenian coast. As pizza has become a favorite dish worldwide, foreign innovations in toppings have often left Italians baffled and appalled. Matteo Martino, a customer at Fiore's pizzeria, said before the expected announcement, "I think, and I hope, that this could be the chance to make foreigners understand how pizza is made, without Nutella or pineapple."

Mr. Trump's failure to deliver on his promise to repeal the Affordable Care Act has made the already daunting task of tax reform even harder. Not only has Mr. Trump's aura of political invincibility been shattered, but without eliminating the Affordable Care Act, Republicans will be unable to overhaul the tax code as sweepingly as the president has demanded. The grand plans for lower rates, fewer loopholes and a tax on imports may need to be scaled back to a large corporate tax cut and perhaps an individual tax cut. Many people think Mr. Trump might settle for this to secure an easy win. “They have to have a victory here,” said Stephen Moore, a Heritage Foundation economist who advised Mr. Trump during the presidential campaign. “But it is going to have to be a bit less ambitious rather than going for the big bang.” Given the arcane rules of lawmaking in Congress, there may be little choice. If Republicans plan to act again without Democratic help, they will need to use a procedure known as budget reconciliation so the Senate can pass tax legislation by a simple majority. For their changes to the tax code to be permanent, their plans cannot add to deficits over a 10-year period. Eliminating the $1 trillion in Affordable Care Act taxes and the federal spending tied to that law would have made this easier.

title: Unwilling to coast on his lead, Trump turns bitter in Republican debate
text: Donald Trump, red-faced with emotion, lashed out at rivals Jeb Bush and Ted Cruz on Saturday in the most acrimonious Republican presidential debate so far, shouting insults and abandoning a promise to be more measured. The New York billionaire came into the CBS debate with momentum, having won New Hampshire last Tuesday and holding a big lead in South Carolina polls a week before Republicans vote there on Feb. 20. Instead of playing it safe, Trump answered every comment aimed at him, interrupted his opponents at will and repeatedly called them liars in an emotional outburst that could raise further questions about whether he has the temperament to serve in the White House. He reserved his harshest attacks for Bush and his brother, former President George W. Bush, who has many admirers in the Republican establishment. It was hard to pick a winner amid the constant barrage of insults, not all of them from Trump. Cruz and fellow Senator Marco Rubio also traded pointed jabs over illegal immigration. But Trump dominated the debate conversation on Twitter with 40 percent of the mentions, according to data from the micro-blogging platform. Trump's combative style has set the tone for much of the campaign, but in recent days he had promised a more measured, positive approach. At the debate, that strategy lasted only through his remarks about Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, who was found dead on Saturday. Trump was quickly provoked when Bush criticized his past statements that Russia has a role to play in Syria. Russia, Bush said, is not attacking Islamic State militants but is instead helping Syrian President Bashir Assad, whom Washington wants to leave power.

title: Trump raises fresh doubts over Russian efforts to influence U.S. election
text: President-elect Donald Trump on Wednesday cast fresh doubt on whether Russian hackers tried to sway the U.S. election in his favor, saying WikiLeaks had denied that Moscow was behind documents it released during the campaign. Writing on Twitter, Trump kept questioning the findings of U.S. intelligence agencies that Russia was responsible for a series of leaks that embarrassed Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton's campaign ahead of the Nov. 8 vote. The tweets led White House spokesman Josh Earnest to ask, “Who are you going to believe?” Documents stolen from the Democratic National Committee and from John Podesta, Clinton's campaign manager, were leaked to the media before the election. One email showed that the Clinton campaign had received a question ahead of a town hall forum. On Wednesday Trump again posted on Twitter about the hacking issue, saying, “(WikiLeaks founder) Julian Assange said ‘a 14 year old could have hacked Podesta’ - why was DNC so careless? Also said the Russians did not give him the info!” Trump also quoted Assange as telling Fox News that U.S. media coverage of the issue was “very dishonest.” Asked about the tweets, Earnest said the president-elect's public comments have set the Russians and Assange against 17 U.S. government intelligence agencies, outside cyber experts and lawmakers from both parties. “There’s a pretty stark line that’s been drawn, and the president-elect will have to determine who he’s going to believe,” he said at a daily news briefing. Vice President-elect Mike Pence defended Trump as simply expressing a “very sincere and healthy American skepticism about intelligence conclusions” he has been hearing. “Given some of the intelligence failures of recent years, the president-elect has made it clear to the American people that he’s skeptical about conclusions from the bureaucracy,” Pence told reporters at the U.S.

title: DONALD TRUMP CLOSES IN ON HILLARY CLINTON IN MICHIGAN
text: Republican nominee Donald Trump is now within striking distance of Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton in Michigan, a state that hasn't backed a Republican presidential candidate since 1988. In the latest Fox 2 Detroit/Mitchell Poll, Trump trails Clinton by just six points. In the four-way poll, Clinton got 48 percent, Trump 42 percent, Libertarian candidate Gary Johnson 4.5 percent, and Green Party candidate Jill Stein 1 percent. In the head-to-head, Clinton led Trump 50 percent to 44 percent. Fifty-nine percent of voters polled said jobs and the economy are the most important issues, while 29 percent said national defense and terrorism matter most. A Detroit Free Press/WXYZ-TV poll puts Clinton ahead of Trump by 7 points, which still represents significant narrowing compared with previous polls. Public backlash against trade deals such as President Barack Obama's Trans-Pacific Partnership - a deal Clinton once called “the gold standard in trade agreements” - was so fierce that Clinton changed her tune during the Democratic primary, where she was beaten by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders. “Across Michigan, Republicans are coming home and taking a united stand against Hillary Clinton’s radical, open-borders agenda and plan to double-down on failed Obama policies, such as Obamacare. We are also seeing independents, Democrats and union workers saying no to Clinton’s special interest driven agenda, and yes to Mr. Trump’s plan to put America first,” Tim Lineberger, communications director for Trump's Michigan campaign team, told The Daily Caller News Foundation.
